newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: CZECH CENTRAL BANK INTENSIFIES BATTLE FOR CROWN.
newsitem.headline: CZECH CENTRAL BANK INTENSIFIES BATTLE FOR CROWN.

text.p: The Czech National Bank (CNB) intensified its week-long battle to shield the crown from speculators on Thursday as hedge funds pushed the currency to record lows.
Analysts forecast the struggle over what used to be central Europe's most stable currency could come to a head in the coming days.
Some said the CNB might be forced to widen or drop altogether the fluctuation band within which it fixes the currency, a key part of Czech currency management since the fall of communism.

The CNB has vowed not to devalue the crown despite wilting confidence in the currency due to a soaring balance of payments deficit and a sharp slowing of Czech economic growth. On Thursday it fought back with market interventions and other steps to choke liquidity.
The CNB moves -- which mirrored those taken by the Thai central bank in recent days as it successfully fended off speculators -- had an immediate effect.

Earlier in the day the crown hit a record low of 6.4 percent below the mid point of a dollar/mark basket which the CNB uses to fix the crown daily. It later rose to about 3.5 percent below following the CNB move.
But analysts said the central bank, with limited reserves and few effective options at its disposal, might be running out of room to manoeuvre.
"This is getting to the end of the line in terms of what you can actually do as a central bank," said Richard Gray, an emerging markets analyst at Bank of America in London.
"There's still reserves certainly but the case for spending reserves on a lost cause is never clear and it all gets resolved quite quickly."
The crown, which has been under pressure for over a week, opened steady on Thursday at about 2.7 percent on the depreciation side of the midpoint.
But speculators in London moved in soon afterward, forcing the central bank to step into the market directly in two waves for the third time in a week.

Dealers said the CNB had also been intervening in London by dealing directly with some foreign banks there, and put estimates of the cost of Thursday's intervention at between $500 million and $1 billion.
The central bank, with immediate effect, also agreed with large domestic banks to limit access by non-resident investors to the Czech money market.
CNB board member Ludek Niedermeyer told Reuters that the central bank was also immediately closing all access to the Lombard credit facility, used by banks to borrow short-term funds.

"This is not a reaction to events only this morning but to the situation that non-residents are taking big positions on the money market. Basically this is increasing the volatility," Niedermeyer said.
The CNB also raised its one-week repurchase rate to 75 percent.

Dealers warned of the cost of maintaining the crown at current levels. This might force the central bank to widen the band in which it fixes the crown to allow the currency to lose value through market forces.
The band is currently 7.5 percent either side of the basket mid point, although in practice the CNB has intervened to defend the crown long before it got anywhere near the edge of the band.

"We know that the economy is weakening and that the central bank is putting rates up, and that's bad news. I think the way out is for wider bands, I think they'll move to 15 percent bands," Stuart Parkinson, an emerging market analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said.
Vladimir Kriedl of Prague-based Patria Finance said: "There is a feeling on the market that the crown is over-valued and our estimation is that it will go down about 10-15 percent in a few days."
"I would say the crisis should be resolved within a few days. Maybe by the middle of next week I think we would see some outcome," he added.
Money market dealers said the central bank tightening moves brought trading to a virtual halt since no funds were available.
But analysts said the moves were only short-term at best, and that the crown would come under fire again when the central bank finally moved to ease its policies.
"I have said that the Czech crown is an accident waiting to happen, and it's now happening. I think that as soon as interest rates go down, the crown goes with them," Gray said.
-- Prague Newsroom, 420-2-2423-0003
